newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo workers told to wait one more day for pay.
newsitem.headline: Congo workers told to wait one more day for pay.

text.p: Civil servants in Laurent Kabila's new Congo, promised cash after months without pay, were told to go away on Wednesday and wait another day.

"It's been put off til tomorrow," a bank cashier said as she closed her counter, turning away a line of hopeful civil servants, grown accustomed to late pay, or no pay at all, under the old regime of president Mobutu Sese Seko.
"So, it's put off for us then. They made us wait all day for nothing. Nothing's changed here at all (since Mobutu)," complained Andre Mampuya.

In a worrying sign for Kabila, who took power in May, the soldiers from his own army, angered by a pay dispute, fired off rounds for up to half an hour in the jungle city of Kisangani in the east on Tuesday, residents and local church radio reported.
They started firing in the crumbling city centre after some were paid in dollars, others in local "Zaire" currency and some not at all, residents said.
The former Zaire has an estimated 600,000 civil servants. Hundreds of them gathered on Wednesday at the public administration building in the capital Kinshasa to claim their meagre wages.
But a sign was slapped on a wall telling them to go to banks to receive the one month's salary they had been promised -- in many cases not much more than $10.
By then, most banks had closed or were closing.
The mood amongst the workers was mostly dejection rather than anger. Many had lost a day's work in the second informal jobs they do to make ends meet.
The legions of civil servants long ago gave up on Mobutu's crumbling state and turned to scraping a living from second jobs, family hand-outs or even wives' prostitution.
Kinkela Pambu earns -- if paid -- $13 a month, but devotes more time to his sideline working for a Ghanaian businessman.

"As a book-keeper, I earn $70 a month. It's not enough, but it helps. I go to my office at Public Administration three times a week. I have some leeway. How can you expect somebody badly and rarely paid to work properly?" he asked, laughing.
The graduate, like many colleagues, relies on his wife who sells cigarettes and vegetables to keep the household together.
Civil servants in the nation of 40 million are angry at getting only one month's pay from the new powers who overthrew Mobutu's 32-year autocracy last month.

They will receive no increase in salary -- but inflation, which touched an annual 900 percent in April, fell to minus 20 percent in May, the month Mobutu fled with the cronies accused of helping him rob the country of its riches.
Finance minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga says civil servants who do not work will be laid off en masse as part of efforts to restore order to a sector full of "fictitious workers".
The heavily indebted state, which receives next to no tax revenue from a chaotic society, will have to pay up from existing funds. They say they will not print new money.
Most people in Africa's third largest country, which Kabila renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, find it hard to make ends meet. Free schooling and health care are pipe dreams.
Some wives of state workers are widely believed to "misbehave" with the consent of their husbands who are constantly out of money.

Decades of economic indiscipline ruined what could have been one of Africa's richest states. Mobutu is said to have stashed away billions of dollars and to have enriched his followers at the expense of the people.
